Abstract
Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-
throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation
within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific
agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data
and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial
intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum
chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a
three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into
structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated,
promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chem-
ical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of
aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA,

1 Introduction
Computational (bio)chemistry has reached a stage of maturity as projects now typically combine
several methods from docking to all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and quantum
chemistry [1]. Quantum-chemical datasets and databases provide a growing resource for this work
[2]. High-performance computing (HPC) resources allow intensive studies with several hundred
quantum-mechanical (QM) calculations, thousands of docking calculations and an interplay with
all-atom MD simulations up to microsecond-range trajectories. This abundance of increasingly

ched . A background
poller sweeps active ssh-slurm runs every 5 minutes, queriessacct for terminal states, auto-fetches
results on completion, and triggerspost_run_assess for automated metric extraction; local runs
are registered in the same run history but are advanced on demand rather than by the poller.
Infrastructure failures (node failures, boot failures, preemption) are distinguished from application
failures; bounded automatic retry for the former is implemented on the development branch. The
job layer can also resume a run in place: a restarted submission reuses the run’s preserved directory
and record, and supported tools continue from intermediate state (for example, a HADDOCK3
restart or a GROMACS checkpoint). Failures that exit successfully but produce wrong results
are not automatically detectable: deciding what to verify is part of the scientific knowledge being
accumulated. Such failures are caught by researcher review against evidence: pre-job validation for
known configuration pitfalls (Section 2.4), and cross-run and literature comparison for scientific
ones (Case Study 4). A class a researcher identifies can then be encoded as an explicit check that
later runs execute. Thecancel_jobtool provides on-demand cancellation.
2.6 Implementation
The memory system is implemented as a Python MCP server (compchem-memory) with modules
for entry management, heuristic retrieval with optional LLM re-ranking, consolidation, session
distillation, and run history tracking. The tool orchestration layer is a separate MCP server
(compchem-tools) with MCP wrappers for the scientific tools the agent drives routinely. The
two servers communicate with the OpenCode agent through the MCP protocol, over stdio for the
memory server and streamable HTTP for the tool server. The agent’s behavior is governed by

a collection of Markdown rule files (rules/) loaded at session start, covering HPC conventions
(remote cluster access, Slurm semantics), job-execution procedures, and operational checklists;
tool-specific protocols (HADDOCK3, GROMACS, P2Rank, xTB, Gnina, Orca, MLAtom) reside in
on-demand skill documents and are retrieved by task relevance. The framework is configured as an
OpenCode workspace; project scaffolding, venv activation, and MCP server startup are handled by
themagnolialaunch wrapper.

4 Memory-System Analysis
Each case study closed with the memory footprint of one campaign. This section examines the store
in aggregate: what the campaigns deposited across projects, how the composition of the largest
store changed over six weeks, and what was elevated from entries into cross-project rules; it closes
with a controlled replay that tests whether what accumulated changes what the agent does.
4.1 Store Composition
Across its four case studies, the Magnolia framework logged 317 tracked runs through its lifecycle
manager (snapshot 2026-09-02; Table 2), spanning HADDOCK3 docking (189 runs), molecular
dynamics of butane and of modified DNA with Amber and MLatom (100 runs), smaller batches
of BindCraft and P2Rank runs (5 runs), and 23 further records with no classified tool. The auto-
extraction pipeline produced 116 project-tier entries in total (human-confirmed or auto-admitted),
distributed across six learning types: 23 scientific findings, 40 general observations and corrections,
14 failure patterns (approach→ failure mode→ lesson), 16 error resolutions (symptoms→ cause
→ fix), 13 parameter guidance entries (specific value→ context), and 10 success patterns (protocol
→result→caveat). Table 3 provides a categorized inventory.
Table 2:Project stores of the four case studies at the snapshot of 2026-09-02. Runs are lifecycle records dated
up to the snapshot; staging and project-tier counts are read from the versioned store histories (index files
excluded). Case Study 1’s benchmark ran as shell-script batches outside the lifecycle manager; it therefore
has no run records. The docking campaign comprises two stores, listed separately; the June–July store is the
one analyzed in Figure 7. Promoted rules are learnings elevated from entries into durable, human-gated rules.
